pages.title: Part 1: Mass, Gravity, and Inertia
pages.readingHtml:
Mass, Weight, and Gravitational Acceleration

All physical objects in the universe are composed of matter. The fundamental measure of the total quantity of matter contained within an object is defined as its mass (m), measured in kilograms (kg). Because matter possesses mass, physical bodies demonstrate an inherent physical resistance to any alteration in their current state of motion—a foundational property known as inertia. Objects with greater mass possess proportionally greater inertia, making them significantly more reluctant to change their state from rest to motion, to accelerate to a higher velocity, or to decelerate to a complete stop.

A critical distinction in biomechanics exists between mass and weight (W). While mass is a scalar quantity measuring inertia, weight is a force vector representing the gravitational pull exerted upon that mass by the Earth (or another celestial body). Weight is quantified in Newtons (N) and is governed by the gravitational acceleration equation:

W = m · g

where m represents mass in kilograms and g represents the acceleration due to gravity, which equals approximately 9.81 m/s2 (or 9.8 m/s2) at Earth's surface. Consequently, an individual's mass remains entirely constant regardless of environmental location, whereas their weight varies directly with gravitational magnitude. In microgravity space environments where g = 0 m/s2, an astronaut experiences a weight of 0 N (weightlessness) while maintaining an identical body mass (m) and linear inertia as on Earth.

Rotational Dynamics and Moment of Inertia

Just as objects translating along a linear path resist changes in linear velocity, rotating bodies possess a reluctance to alter their state of angular motion—a property termed angular inertia. In rotational biomechanics, this rotational reluctance is measured by the moment of inertia (I). Unlike linear inertia, which depends exclusively on total mass, the moment of inertia depends upon two distinct physical factors:

  • Total Mass (m): The total mass of the rotating body or segment.
  • Mass Distribution (r or k): How that mass is spatially distributed relative to the specific axis of rotation, quantified as the radius of gyration (k) or distance (r). Mathematically, I = m · k2.

Because the distance factor (k) is squared in the moment of inertia equation, altering the spatial distribution of mass relative to the axis of rotation exerts a profound exponential effect on rotational resistance. For example, comparing a soccer ball to a tennis ball, the soccer ball possesses greater rotational inertia not only because it has greater mass, but also because its larger diameter places its mass farther from its central axis of rotation.

In human movement, athletes dynamically manipulate their body's moment of inertia by altering limb posture around an axis of rotation passing through their center of mass. In diving, gymnastics, and figure skating, executing a dive or flip in a layout position extends the body segments far from the rotational axis, resulting in a large moment of inertia (I) that makes rotation slow and difficult to initiate or accelerate. Conversely, pulling the limbs inward into a tight tuck position dramatically concentrates body mass closer to the axis of rotation, drastically reducing I and enabling rapid angular acceleration and high rotational velocity.

Clinical / Coaching Application

In high-platform diving and acrobatic gymnastics, coaches utilize the physics of moment of inertia (I = m · k2) to teach aerial spin control. When a diver transitions from takeoff into a somersault, their angular momentum remains conserved. By flexing at the hips and knees to adopt a tight tuck position, the diver reduces their radius of gyration (k), decreasing their moment of inertia (I) by up to 300% to 400%. This dramatic reduction in rotational resistance causes an immediate inverse surge in angular velocity, allowing the athlete to complete triple somersaults before opening back into a layout position (increasing I) to slow down rotation for a clean water entry.

pages.title: Part 2: Types of Motion
pages.readingHtml:
Fundamental Classifications of Human Motion

Human movement encompasses a wide spectrum of physical trajectories and mechanical behaviors. To systematically analyze human movement, biomechanists differentiate between three primary classifications of motion: linear motion, angular motion, and general motion.

Linear Motion (Translation)

Linear motion, frequently termed translation, occurs when all parts of a body or system move the exact same distance, in the exact same direction, and at the exact same time. During pure linear translation, the body moves as a unified whole without individual segment parts moving in relation to one another. Linear movement patterns are further sub-classified based on the geometric shape of the travel path:

  • Rectilinear Motion: Linear translation along a straight, unvarying line path. Classic examples include a sprinter's 100-meter straightaway dash, a toboggan sliding down a straight ice track, or a dropped ball falling purely vertically under gravity.
  • Curvilinear Motion: Linear translation along a curved path, where all points of the system travel along parallel curved trajectories. Examples include the parabolic flight path of a ski jumper through the air, a thrown discus trajectory, or a hit baseball traveling through the outfield.

Angular Motion (Rotation)

Angular motion, also referred to as rotation, occurs when a body or system moves along a circular path in the same direction about a central line or pivot point termed the axis of rotation. During angular motion, points on the body located farther from the axis of rotation travel greater linear distances than points closer to the axis, even though all points sweep through identical angular displacements (degrees or radians).

In human movement, rotation occurs about both external and internal axes:

  • External Axes of Rotation: Rotating around an axis located outside the physical body, such as a gymnast executing giant swings around a high bar or an automobile wheel turning on its axle.
  • Internal Joint Axes of Rotation: Body segments rotating around anatomical joint axes (e.g., flexion, extension, abduction, and longitudinal axial rotation). Examples include forearm rotation during a tennis serve or hip rotation during a golf swing.

General Motion: The Universal Combination

While linear translation and angular rotation represent pure mechanical categories, the vast majority of human athletic skills and everyday physical activities consist of general motion. General motion is defined as a complex combination of linear motion and angular motion occurring simultaneously (i.e., a body translating linearly through space while its individual segments rotate around joint axes).

For example, in running, the athlete's total body center of mass translates linearly down the track (general linear motion), while their lower limbs execute continuous angular rotations (flexion, extension) around the hip, knee, and ankle joint axes. Similarly, a gymnast performing a floor routine or a diver executing a somersault while falling vertically toward the pool exemplifies general motion.

Clinical / Coaching Application

Understanding general motion is essential for analyzing the kinematic chain in high-velocity throwing and striking sports (e.g., baseball pitching, tennis serving, javelin throwing). While the ultimate objective is to maximize the linear velocity of the projectile (a linear outcome), this is achieved through a precisely timed kinetic chain sequence of angular rotations. Rotation originates in the large proximal segments (pelvis and trunk around the spine) and transfers sequentially to smaller distal levers (shoulder, elbow, wrist). A coach evaluating a pitcher uses general motion principles to ensure distal linear speed is created by proximal joint rotation rather than arm strain.

pages.title: Part 3: Causes of Motion and Lever Systems
pages.readingHtml:
Causes of Motion: Forces, Centric Actions, and Torque

As established in physical mechanics, the ultimate cause of any body motion is the application of forces. A force is defined as any action—a push or a pull—that tends to alter an object's state of motion by producing an acceleration (F = m · a). If an object experiences zero net force, it remains in a state of constant velocity (where rest is simply a constant velocity of 0 m/s). Forces acting on the human body are classified as either internal (muscular contractions, joint cartilage reaction forces) or external (gravity, ground reaction forces, fluid resistance).

The spatial line of action through which a force is applied determines whether the resulting motion is linear or angular:

  • Centric Force: A force whose line of action passes directly through an object's center of mass. Centric forces produce pure linear motion (translation) without rotation, such as pushing a cart straight from its center or throwing a ball directly through its midpoint.
  • Eccentric (Off-Center) Force: A force whose line of action does not pass through the object's center of mass or axis of rotation. Eccentric forces produce a turning effect, causing the object to experience angular acceleration and rotate about an axis.

When an eccentric force produces angular motion around an axis, the resulting turning effect is termed a moment of force, or torque. Torque (τ) is the rotary equivalent of linear force and represents the quantitative turning capacity of a force.

Anatomical Lever Systems and Torque Mechanics

The fundamental structural arrangement required to produce angular motion is a lever system. A lever system consists of a rigid bar (the lever) that rotates around a fixed pivot point or axis of rotation (A), also known as the fulcrum. In human anatomy, bones function as rigid levers, joint articulations function as axes of rotation, and skeletal muscle contractions generate applied forces or resistive loads.

Angular motion occurs whenever the applied turning force generates a torque that exceeds the resistive torque opposing rotation at the axis. Calculating torque requires measuring two specific perpendicular distances from the axis of rotation:

  • Force Arm (FA): The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of application of the applied force.
  • Resistance Arm (RA): The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of application of the resistance or weight.

The magnitude of torque produced by a lever system is calculated using the fundamental equation:

Torque = Force Arm × Force   (τ = FA · F)

This formula demonstrates that a lever's mechanical advantage is directly governed by the length of its force arm. Extending the force arm increases the leverage, allowing a smaller applied force to generate substantial torque. In human anatomy, muscle insertion sites are located very close to joint axes, resulting in extremely short force arms (FA). This structural arrangement puts human muscles at a distinct mechanical disadvantage for force production, requiring muscles to exert immense tension to lift modest external weights.

Classification of Levers: First, Second, and Third Class

Levers are categorized into three distinct classes based on the relative anatomical positioning of the axis (A), applied force (F), and resistance (R):

First Class Levers (F - A - R)

In a first class lever, the axis of rotation (A) is positioned between the applied force (F) and the resistance (R). First class levers can balance forces, change force direction, or alter speed depending on force arm lengths. In everyday life, scissors, crowbars, and teeter-totters are first class levers. In human anatomy, flexion and extension of the head about the atlanto-occipital joint (C1) is a classic first class lever (neck extensor muscles supply force on one side of C1, while skull weight acts as resistance on the opposite side). The simultaneous action of agonist and antagonist muscles across a joint axis also forms a first class lever system.

Second Class Levers (A - R - F)

In a second class lever, the resistance (R) is positioned between the axis (A) and the applied force (F), meaning the force arm (FA) is always longer than the resistance arm (RA). Second class levers always provide a mechanical advantage for force (MA > 1), allowing a small force to move a heavy load. Everyday examples include wheelbarrows, nutcrackers, and bottle openers. Second class levers are extremely rare in human anatomy; raising the body onto the toes via gastrocnemius/soleus contraction (where the metatarsophalangeal joint axis is at one end, body weight resistance acts in the middle, and calf tendon force pulls at the heel) serves as a primary example.

Third Class Levers (A - F - R)

In a third class lever, the applied force (F) is positioned between the axis (A) and the resistance (R), meaning the force arm (FA) is shorter than the resistance arm (RA). Third class levers operate at a mechanical disadvantage for force (MA < 1), requiring large muscle forces to move small loads. However, third class levers provide an extraordinary mechanical advantage for speed and range of motion, allowing distal extremities to move rapidly through wide arcs. Everyday examples include tweezers, brooms, and snow shovels. Most musculoskeletal lever systems in the human body operate as third class levers during concentric contractions (e.g., biceps brachii flexing the forearm, hamstrings flexing the knee, running gait, and throwing mechanics).

Clinical / Coaching Application

The overwhelming prevalence of third-class levers in human anatomy reveals a fundamental evolutionary design trade-off: the human body is engineered for high-velocity movement and extensive range of motion rather than brute force. Because muscle tendons insert close to joint axes (short FA), a small muscle shortening distance produces a massive, high-velocity angular sweep at the hand or foot. In strength and conditioning, coaches must recognize that during a biceps curl or leg extension, the mechanical torque demand changes across the joint range of motion as the perpendicular force arm changes, reaching peak torque requirement when the resistive load line forms a 90° angle relative to the lever bone.

The inherent property of matter that causes an object to resist any change in its current state of motion or rest.
The quantitative measure of a rotating body's resistance to changes in its angular motion, governed by total mass and its spatial distribution relative to the axis of rotation (I = m * k^2).

Movement of a body along a circular path in the same direction around a central axis of rotation; also termed rotation.

Any push or pull action applied to a body that tends to alter its state of motion by causing an acceleration.
The rotary turning effect produced when a force is applied off-center (eccentrically) relative to an axis of rotation; calculated as Torque = Force Arm * Force.
A mechanical device consisting of a rigid bar (lever) that rotates around a fixed pivot point or axis of rotation (fulcrum) when force is applied.
The perpendicular distance measured from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the applied force.
The perpendicular distance measured from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the resistance load or weight.
A lever classification in which the axis of rotation is positioned between the applied force and the resistance (F-A-R).
